etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English in, inn, from Old English inn (“a dwelling, house, chamber, lodging”); akin to Icelandic inni (“a dwelling place, home, abode”), Faroese inni (“home”).

definitions.definition: Any establishment where travellers can procure lodging, food, and drink.

quote.citation: 1824, Geoffrey Crayon [pseudonym; Washington Irving], “The Adventure of My Uncle”, in Tales of a Traveller, part 1 (Strange Stories. […]), Philadelphia, Pa.: H[enry] C[harles] Carey & I[saac] Lea, […], →OCLC, page 21:
quote.text: [H]ow much more agreeable to himself to get into snug quarters in a chateau, [...] rather than take up with the miserable lodgement, and miserable fare of a country inn.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter IV, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC, pages 46–47:
quote.text: One morning I had been driven to the precarious refuge afforded by the steps of the inn, after rejecting offers from the Celebrity to join him in a variety of amusements. But even here I was not free from interruption, for he was seated on a horse-block below me, playing with a fox terrier.

definitions.definition: One of the colleges (societies or buildings) in London, for students of the law barristers.
(British, dated) The town residence of a nobleman or distinguished person.
(obsolete) A place of shelter; hence, dwelling, residence, abode.

quote.citation: 1579, Immeritô [pseudonym; Edmund Spenser], “Nouember. Ægloga Vndecima.”, in The Shepheardes Calender: […], London:  […]  Hugh Singleton, […], →OCLC, folio 44, verso:
quote.text: But nowe ſadde Winter welked hath the day, / And Phœbus weary of his yerely taſ-ke: / Yſtabled hath his ſteedes in lowlye laye / And taken vp his ynne in Fiſhes haſ-ke.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 33, page 12:
quote.text: Therefore with me ye may take vp your In / For this ſame night.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, intransitive) To take lodging; to lodge or house oneself.

quote.citation: 1714 March 16 (Gregorian calendar), Joseph Addison, “The Free-holder: No. 22. Friday, March 5. [1714.]”, in The Works of the Right Honourable Joseph Addison, Esq; […], volume IV, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], published 1721, →OCLC:
quote.text: But where do you intend to inn to-night?
We inned at the signe of the Swan.

quote.citation: 1606, Sir G. Goosecappe I, iii, in Bullen O. Pl. III:
quote.text: I never innd in the Towne but once.
John Welch, Cornish Carrier, who formerly Inn'd at the Mermaid in Exon, is now removed to the Bear-Inn.

quote.citation: 1885, M. J. Colquhoun, Primes in Indis, I, xiv, 217:
quote.text: I inned at the best house, the Star and Garter.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To lodge or house (someone or something).

quote.citation: 2018 [1607], Thomas Middleton, Michaelmas term and a trick to catch the old one, Walter de Gruyter GmbH & Co KG, →ISBN, page 27:
quote.text: I have but Inn'd my horse since, master Cockstone.

quote.citation: 1710, New Map Trav. High Church Apostle, 7, quoted in 1901, James Augustus Henry Murray, A New English Dictionary on Historical Principles: part 1. H (1901), page 309:
quote.text: These Inn'd themselves all Night in Knights-bridge Fields.
